paragraphs: LEO is an agent designed to understand and act in three-dimensional environments. The paper addresses a gap in general-purpose models: many can interpret images but have limited support for 3D inputs and tasks that require spatial understanding. These tasks include connecting language to objects in a scene, reasoning about an environment, and deciding how to move or manipulate objects.

The researchers train LEO using a shared task interface, architecture, and learning objective. Training first aligns 3D visual information with language, then uses instructions to connect vision and language with actions. They also assemble large datasets covering individual objects and whole scenes, and build a language-model-assisted pipeline for producing 3D vision-language training data.

Experiments demonstrate capabilities across captioning, question answering, embodied reasoning, navigation, and manipulation. The breadth of these evaluations supports the idea that one agent can learn several complementary 3D skills through a unified setup. Ablation studies and scaling analyses additionally examine the system’s development, providing evidence intended to inform future embodied generalist agents.
icml-2024-an-embodied-generalist-agent-i.tldr: LEO combines 3D vision, language, and action training in one agent that handles diverse spatial understanding and interaction tasks.

paragraphs: Counterfactual estimation asks what might have happened under a different treatment or decision, using observations of what actually occurred. A central difficulty is treatment bias: groups receiving different treatments can differ in other relevant characteristics. Balancing strategies try to reduce these differences so that comparisons between treatment groups are more informative.

This paper examines whether that strategy works effectively when observations form time series. The authors revisit counterfactual estimation in this temporal setting and summarize recent balancing approaches. Their main contribution is an empirical investigation across multiple datasets and settings, focused on the effectiveness, robustness, and applicability of balancing rather than introducing a new estimation method.

The findings lead the authors to call for reconsidering how balancing is used with time-series data. That conclusion questions the transfer of a broadly used strategy into temporal problems; it does not establish that balancing always fails. The practical significance is that reducing differences between treatment groups deserves direct evaluation in temporal estimation, rather than being treated as sufficient evidence that the counterfactual estimates will improve.
icml-2024-an-empirical-examination-of-ba.tldr: An empirical study across datasets calls for reexamining the effectiveness of balancing strategies for time-series counterfactual estimation.

paragraphs: AttNS addresses a problem in numerical methods that combine conventional solvers with learned components: limited training data can weaken their generalization and robustness when solving differential equations. The paper proposes a compact, attention-inspired modification intended to improve existing solvers without requiring elaborate model design.

The method draws inspiration from attention modules used in residual neural networks. By interpreting those networks through a dynamical-systems perspective, the authors adapt attention mechanisms to the structure of numerical equation solving. This connection matters because it gives a route for incorporating a successful learning mechanism into numerical methods while still considering the solver’s mathematical behavior.

Benchmarks covering high-dimensional problems and chaotic systems show improvements across multiple numerical solvers. The paper combines experiments and theory to support strong generalization and robustness together with solver convergence. In the reported comparisons, AttNS needs less data to reach comparable generalization errors and better prevents numerical explosions. These findings position it as a way to make learned numerical solving more dependable when training examples are scarce.
icml-2024-attns-attention-inspired-numer.tldr: AttNS incorporates attention-inspired mechanisms into numerical solvers to improve generalization and stability with limited training data.

paragraphs: Bayesian Power Steering, or BPS, adapts large pretrained diffusion models to more specific tasks. The paper frames this adaptation as moving from a broad probability space to a narrower one: the pretrained model contains knowledge about many possible outputs, while the new task requires a more focused part of that knowledge.

The authors use a Bayesian perspective to explain how learnable modules can extract task-specific knowledge from the model’s learned prior distribution. Their proposed network structure intervenes differently in different hidden features, using what they describe as a head-heavy, foot-light configuration. The central design choice is therefore uneven intervention across the model’s internal features, rather than treating every feature identically during adaptation.

Experiments report better results than contemporary approaches across several tasks, including settings with limited data. One stated result is an FID score of 10.49 for sketch-conditioned generation on COCO17. Taken together, the findings support the usefulness of selective adaptation for extracting relevant capabilities from a large diffusion model when task-specific training data are limited.
icml-2024-bayesian-power-steering-an-eff.tldr: BPS uses Bayesian reasoning and selective intervention in hidden features to adapt pretrained diffusion models, with strong reported results under limited data.

paragraphs: BiLLM compresses pretrained language-model weights to roughly one bit each while trying to preserve useful prediction quality. Such aggressive compression targets the substantial memory and computation demands of large models. The challenge is that existing quantization methods struggle to retain performance when each weight has so few representable values.

The method treats weights differently according to their importance and distribution. It identifies structurally selected salient weights and uses a binary residual approximation to reduce compression loss. For the remaining weights, whose distribution is bell-shaped, it searches for a split that groups them for more accurate binarization. This separates two compression problems that would otherwise be handled with one uniform rule.

The reported results include perplexity of 8.41 on LLaMA2-70B with an effective weight precision of 1.08 bits, alongside substantial improvements over competing quantization methods across evaluated model families and metrics. A 7-billion-parameter model can be binarized within half an hour on one GPU. That timing measures the compression procedure, while the quality results demonstrate the feasibility of inference at extremely low weight precision.
icml-2024-billm-pushing-the-limit-of-pos.tldr: BiLLM uses separate binarization strategies for salient and other weights to compress language models to 1.08-bit weights with strong reported accuracy.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks process information through discrete spikes and offer promise for energy-efficient temporal processing. Their discrete outputs also make training difficult because the spiking operation is not differentiable. Surrogate gradients provide a way to train these networks, but their accuracy often remains below that of conventional artificial neural networks.

This paper investigates that gap in networks built from leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. Analytical and experimental studies connect degraded accuracy to gradients fading as they propagate through time. The proposed complementary leaky integrate-and-fire neuron, CLIF, adds paths that help temporal gradients travel during backpropagation while preserving binary outputs. The neuron design is also described as hyperparameter-free.

Experiments across several datasets show a clear performance advantage over other neuron models. Under matched network structures and training conditions, CLIF even slightly exceeds the performance of strong conventional neural networks in the reported evaluations. The contribution links a specific training difficulty to a neuron-level modification, showing that improving temporal gradient flow can substantially narrow the accuracy gap.
icml-2024-clif-complementary-leaky-integ.tldr: CLIF adds temporal gradient paths to spiking neurons, improving reported accuracy while retaining binary outputs.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction expresses uncertainty by returning a set of possible labels with a desired coverage guarantee. For deep classifiers, inaccurate probability estimates can make these sets unnecessarily large. A large set may still contain the correct answer, but it gives the user less precise information about which label applies.

The paper introduces Sorted Adaptive Prediction Sets, or SAPS, to reduce reliance on those probability values. It retains the maximum softmax probability and discards the other probability magnitudes, using label ranking in constructing prediction sets. The aim is to preserve information about an example’s uncertainty while making the non-conformity score less dependent on potentially miscalibrated numerical probabilities.

Experiments show that SAPS produces smaller prediction sets and broadly improves conditional coverage rates. The latter is an empirical finding about coverage beyond an overall aggregate, rather than a stated universal conditional-coverage guarantee. The approach matters because it suggests that retaining every probability value is not required for useful uncertainty estimates: ranking information and a limited confidence signal can support compact, informative sets.
icml-2024-conformal-prediction-for-deep-.tldr: SAPS relies on label ranking and the maximum predicted probability to produce smaller conformal prediction sets with improved empirical conditional coverage.

paragraphs: Weather forecasting depends on a good estimate of the atmosphere’s starting state. Data assimilation creates that estimate by combining model predictions with observations. DiffDA approaches this task with a denoising diffusion model that uses predicted atmospheric states and sparse measurements to generate an atmospheric state consistent with the observations.

The authors adapt the pretrained GraphCast network as the diffusion model’s backbone, drawing on the similarity between weather prediction and atmospheric denoising. In experiments using simulated observations from ERA5 reanalysis, DiffDA produces global atmospheric data at 0.25-degree resolution, approximately 30 kilometers. The paper reports this as the highest resolution achieved by machine-learning data assimilation models.

Using observations covering less than 0.96% of the grid together with a 48-hour forecast, DiffDA generates initial conditions that support subsequent forecasting. Relative to initialization from ERA5’s state-of-the-art assimilation, the reported loss of forecast lead time is at most 24 hours. These simulated-observation results support potential applications such as repeatedly assimilating data to construct reanalysis datasets.
icml-2024-diffda-a-diffusion-model-for-w.tldr: DiffDA combines sparse observations and forecasts through a GraphCast-based diffusion model to generate high-resolution global atmospheric initial conditions.

paragraphs: Agents in mixed-motive environments must adapt to other participants whose interests can involve both cooperation and competition. Predicting those participants is useful only if the agent can turn its predictions into effective decisions. HOP addresses both parts of this problem, aiming to adapt after relatively few interactions with previously unseen policies.

Its hierarchical structure contains an opponent-modeling module and a planning module. The first infers other agents’ goals and learns policies conditioned on those goals. The second uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to search for a best response. Beliefs about others’ goals are updated both during an episode and across episodes, while the learned opponent information guides planning.

Experiments show superior few-shot adaptation when HOP interacts with various unseen agents in mixed-motive environments, as well as strong performance in self-play. The authors also report the emergence of social intelligence in their experiments. Together, these results suggest that inferring goals can be especially useful when that inference directly shapes planning and is revised as interactions unfold.
icml-2024-efficient-adaptation-in-mixed-.tldr: HOP combines goal-based opponent modeling with tree-search planning to adapt quickly to unfamiliar agents in mixed-motive environments.

paragraphs: A graph neural network may accept graphs of many sizes yet classify larger graphs poorly if training involved smaller ones. This paper focuses on that distinction between being able to process an input and generalizing well to it. The authors identify size information remaining in learned graph representations as a problem insufficiently addressed by existing approaches.

DISGEN is a model-agnostic framework that separates size-related factors from graph representations. It uses augmentations with size- and task-invariance properties, together with a decoupling loss that reduces shared information in hidden representations. The intent is to disentangle information about graph size from information useful for the classification task. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for the effectiveness of this mechanism.

On real-world datasets, the authors report improvements of up to 6% over state-of-the-art models. This is the largest reported improvement, rather than a uniform gain across every setting. The findings support disentanglement as a way to improve generalization to larger graphs without making the approach specific to a single backbone architecture.
icml-2024-enhancing-size-generalization-.tldr: DISGEN separates graph-size information from learned representations to improve classification on graphs larger than those seen during training.

paragraphs: Spectral graph neural networks use graph filters to control how information moves through a graph. Polynomial filters avoid the expensive eigendecomposition used by optimal spectral filters, but many rely on polynomial bases that stay fixed across graphs. This can be restrictive when graphs differ in heterophily, the extent to which connected nodes have different characteristics or labels.

The paper theoretically analyzes how suitable polynomial bases relate to a graph’s degree of heterophily. It then constructs an adaptive basis whose vectors form angles reflecting that degree. Combining this with a homophily basis produces UniBasis, which supports a polynomial-filter graph neural network called UniFilter. The design makes the filter’s building blocks responsive to graph structure.

The authors report that this approach limits over-smoothing and alleviates over-squashing, two problems affecting information propagation in graph networks. Experiments across datasets with different degrees of heterophily support the basis’s broad applicability and usefulness for graph explanation. The contribution connects a mathematical property of the filter basis to the kinds of neighborhood relationships present in the data.
icml-2024-how-universal-polynomial-bases.tldr: UniBasis adapts polynomial graph filters to heterophily, supporting broad graph performance while reducing propagation problems.

paragraphs: In-context reinforcement learning can let an offline-trained model improve during online interaction by reading experience in its prompt, without updating its weights. However, representing trial and error as a sequence spanning multiple episodes becomes expensive when tasks require many actions. Longer task horizons make the context increasingly costly to process.

The In-context Decision Transformer, or IDT, changes the level at which this experience is represented. Its sequence contains high-level decisions, each capable of guiding several low-level actions in the environment. This hierarchical organization allows trial-and-error improvement to operate over a shorter decision sequence, reducing the need to represent every environmental action at the same level.

Experiments report state-of-the-art results on long-horizon tasks relative to the evaluated in-context reinforcement-learning methods. Online evaluation is reported as 36 times faster than baselines on D4RL and 27 times faster on Grid World. These findings show that restructuring the decision sequence can substantially improve evaluation efficiency while supporting strong performance on tasks requiring extended interaction.
icml-2024-in-context-decision-transforme.tldr: IDT represents experience through high-level decisions, enabling faster in-context reinforcement learning on long-horizon tasks.

paragraphs: InstructSpeech aims to edit both what speech says and how it sounds by following natural-language instructions. To address scarce training data, the researchers construct examples pairing an instruction with input and output speech. These triplets train a multitask language model to connect a requested change with the corresponding audio transformation.

The system combines learned task embeddings with a fine-tuned Flan-T5-XL model to guide generation toward the appropriate task. Training covers diverse speech editing and processing tasks, and the authors investigate chain-of-thought reasoning for free-form changes to semantic content. A hierarchical adapter supports generalization to new tasks by updating only a small portion of the model’s parameters.

The paper also introduces an evaluation benchmark using contrastive instruction-speech pretraining to assess speech quality and how faithfully the output follows the instruction. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on eleven tasks. The contribution brings instruction interpretation, acoustic editing, and content editing into one framework, with evaluation explicitly considering whether the resulting speech matches the user’s requested transformation.
icml-2024-instructspeech-following-speec.tldr: InstructSpeech learns to modify speech content and acoustic attributes from natural-language instructions, reporting state-of-the-art results on eleven tasks.

paragraphs: IRDiff generates three-dimensional ligand molecules for specific protein targets. The paper addresses a difficulty with generating molecules entirely from scratch: without suitable reference ligands, optimization can be challenging and the generated molecules may be suboptimal. Its approach uses retrieved examples with desirable properties to guide the generation process.

A protein-molecule interaction network, PMINet, is pretrained using binding-affinity signals. It retrieves target-aware ligands with high binding affinity from a curated reference collection. It also supplies information about important protein-ligand binding structures to steer diffusion-based generation. The model incorporates this guidance through two mechanisms described as retrieval augmentation and self augmentation.

Experiments on CrossDocked2020 show more realistic generated 3D structures and state-of-the-art binding affinities toward the evaluated protein targets, while retaining appropriate molecular properties. These findings support reference-guided generation as a useful direction for structure-based drug design. The central contribution is to make the references relevant to the target’s interactions, so that retrieved molecular knowledge can influence the structures the diffusion model generates.
icml-2024-interaction-based-retrieval-au.tldr: IRDiff retrieves target-relevant ligand references to guide diffusion-based 3D molecule generation, improving reported structure quality and binding affinity.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised image classification uses a small labeled dataset alongside unlabeled images. Many methods combine a supervised classification loss with a separate regularization term derived only from unlabeled data. InterLUDE examines what can be gained by allowing the labeled and unlabeled examples to interact more directly during learning.

It introduces two complementary mechanisms. Embedding fusion interpolates between representations of labeled and unlabeled images, linking the two data sources during representation learning. A second component adds a consistency-based loss that reduces discrepancies between predictions for labeled and unlabeled inputs. Both components are designed around the relationship between the data groups, rather than only adding their separate training objectives.

Experiments show benefits on standard closed-set semi-supervised benchmarks and a medical task with an uncurated unlabeled dataset. On STL-10 with only 40 labels, InterLUDE achieves a 3.2% error rate, compared with 6.3% reported for the best previous method. The results support using labeled-unlabeled interactions in both representations and predictions to make limited labeled data more effective.
icml-2024-interlude-interactions-between.tldr: InterLUDE improves semi-supervised learning by mixing labeled and unlabeled representations and encouraging consistency between their predictions.

paragraphs: Machine Vision Therapy uses multimodal language models to help correct the predictions of vision models under distribution shifts. Models such as CLIP can generalize well yet remain unreliable on unfamiliar data. The proposed approach uses multimodal-model predictions as supervision, aiming to improve robustness with very little reliance on human annotation.

A key obstacle is that a multimodal language model may not naturally handle the vision task in the required way. Denoising In-Context Learning addresses this mismatch by estimating examples’ noise probabilities through a transition matrix. It constructs an instruction containing a correct example and a likely incorrect one, helping the model identify and repair erroneous vision-model predictions.

The paper proves that this procedure can find the ground truth under assumptions described as mild. That guarantee remains conditional on those assumptions. Experiments across several out-of-distribution datasets show improvements in visual robustness in many settings. The approach therefore combines a method for eliciting useful corrections with a training strategy that transfers those corrections back to the vision model.
icml-2024-machine-vision-therapy-multimo.tldr: Machine Vision Therapy uses carefully constructed multimodal prompts to correct vision-model predictions and improve robustness under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Hyperspectral image super-resolution combines a spatially coarse hyperspectral image with a sharper multispectral image to produce a high-resolution hyperspectral result. The two inputs contain different kinds of features. Ignoring that mismatch can distort spectral information and blur spatial textures, even when the purpose of fusion is to improve both.

MFTN addresses this with feature extraction, transfer, and aggregation at multiple scales. Three feature extractors first obtain representations at different scales. A transfer module containing three improved feature-matching Transformers learns correlations between the low-resolution hyperspectral image and a degraded multispectral image. Those correlations guide the transfer of detail from the high-resolution multispectral input.

A dynamic aggregation module then gradually combines the transferred features, using three spectral-aware aggregation modules to reconstruct the final image. Experiments on three commonly used datasets report better performance than state-of-the-art methods. The design’s significance lies in explicitly matching features across the two image types before combining their information, while keeping multiple spatial scales and spectral characteristics involved in reconstruction.
icml-2024-mftn-a-multi-scale-feature-tra.tldr: MFTN matches and transfers features across image types and scales to improve hyperspectral image super-resolution.

paragraphs: MLAgentBench evaluates whether language-model agents can carry out machine-learning experimentation: designing experiments, running them, inspecting results, and iterating toward an objective. Its thirteen tasks range from improving CIFAR-10 performance to research problems such as BabyLM. Agents can read and write files, execute code, and examine the resulting outputs.

The researchers build an experimentation agent using the ReAct framework and compare versions powered by several language models. The Claude v3 Opus agent has the highest reported success rate, averaging 37.5%, and produces compelling models on many tasks. The agents’ plans and actions are also described as highly interpretable, allowing their experimental behavior to be examined.

Performance varies sharply across tasks, from 100% success on established older datasets to 0% on recent Kaggle challenges that may have been created after model training. The paper identifies long-term planning and hallucination reduction as key challenges. These results demonstrate useful experimentation capabilities while showing that success on familiar task settings does not establish reliable performance across newer research problems.
icml-2024-mlagentbench-evaluating-langua.tldr: MLAgentBench tests autonomous machine-learning experimentation and finds useful but highly uneven capabilities across thirteen tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much data model-based reinforcement learning needs to find a Nash equilibrium in mean-field games. The setting requires strategic exploration and function approximation for the model. The central question is whether learning equilibrium behavior in this multi-agent setting necessarily demands much more experience than single-agent reinforcement learning.

The authors introduce Partial Model-Based Eluder Dimension, or P-MBED, to measure model-class complexity through an associated single-agent model class. This measure can potentially be exponentially smaller than the earlier MBED measure. They then develop a model-elimination algorithm with a new exploration strategy and prove sample-complexity bounds that are polynomial in P-MBED.

Under realizability and Lipschitz continuity assumptions, the resulting statistical difficulty is no greater than solving a logarithmic number of single-agent reinforcement-learning problems. The theory also extends to mean-field games with multiple agent types. Separately, the authors develop and empirically evaluate a more computationally efficient heuristic inspired by the theoretical algorithm. This distinction matters: the main equivalence concerns data requirements, while computational efficiency receives additional treatment.
icml-2024-model-based-rl-for-mean-field-.tldr: Under realizability and Lipschitz assumptions, learning mean-field-game equilibria needs no more data than a logarithmic number of single-agent RL problems.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks rely on a local label-smoothness assumption: nearby nodes tend to have similar labels. Their feature-smoothing operation reflects that expectation. This paper examines nodes for which smoothing produces labels that conflict with the assumption, identifying cases where both the assumption and the smoothing process become problematic.

The authors call these cases out-of-control, or OOC, nodes. They design an algorithm to locate them, study characteristics that affect how their representations are learned, and use those observations to develop DaGCN. This framework targets the problematic nodes, making the analysis of individual node behavior central to the model improvement.

Experiments support DaGCN’s performance advantage and suggest that improvements from advanced GCNs are concentrated on OOC nodes. For the remaining under-control nodes, the authors find that a basic GCN already provides optimal representations on most evaluated datasets. This finding motivates a more selective view of graph-network design: understanding where smoothing breaks down can identify which nodes need additional modeling support.
icml-2024-on-which-nodes-does-gcn-fail-e.tldr: DaGCN identifies and improves nodes where ordinary graph convolution’s label-smoothness assumption and feature smoothing break down.

paragraphs: Decentralized federated learning lets clients train their own models without a central server. Clients may use different architectures and hold differently distributed data, creating a challenge for learning representations that generalize beyond each local dataset. Without a shared global model, exchanging useful knowledge between those clients becomes particularly important.

DeSA introduces synthetic anchors derived from raw-data distributions to support that exchange. Drawing on domain adaptation and knowledge distillation, the paper provides theoretical and empirical evidence that these anchors facilitate mutual knowledge transfer. They serve as common reference information through which separately trained local models can benefit from one another.

Two training losses make this concrete. A regularization loss aligns each client’s latent-representation distribution with the anchors, while a knowledge-distillation loss lets clients learn from others. Experiments across diverse client-data distributions report improvements in each client’s accuracy both within and across domains. The contribution is a shared synthetic reference mechanism for improving local models despite differences in both their data and their architectures.
icml-2024-overcoming-data-and-model-hete.tldr: DeSA uses synthetic anchors and two training losses to transfer knowledge between decentralized clients with different data and models.

paragraphs: TrustLLM organizes language-model trustworthiness into principles, benchmarks, and empirical evaluation. It proposes principles across eight dimensions and builds a benchmark covering six: truthfulness, safety, fairness, robustness, privacy, and machine ethics. The evaluation includes sixteen mainstream models and more than thirty datasets, treating trustworthiness as a collection of distinct concerns.

The study finds that functional capability and trustworthiness are generally positively related. Proprietary models generally outperform most open-source models in the evaluation, but some open-source systems come close. The authors interpret those exceptions as evidence that open-source models can achieve high trustworthiness without additional mechanisms such as a moderator.

The paper also observes that some models refuse benign prompts after mistakenly treating them as harmful, sacrificing usefulness through excessive caution. Its findings therefore concern both harmful behavior and unnecessary restrictions on legitimate use. Beyond evaluation, the authors advocate transparency in models and in the technologies used to support trustworthiness, along with collaboration among industry, academia, and the open-source community.
icml-2024-position-trustllm-trustworthin.tldr: TrustLLM evaluates multiple dimensions of language-model trustworthiness, finding broad capability correlations alongside model differences and unnecessary refusals.

paragraphs: Random-feature methods make kernel techniques faster by replacing a kernel with a finite feature representation. The usual construction uses Monte Carlo sampling, so approximation quality depends on how many features are generated. This paper asks whether replacing that sampling method with quasi-Monte Carlo can provide better accuracy for the same representation size.

For a class of kernels that includes Gaussian kernels, the authors prove an improvement from error scaling as O_P(1/√M) to O(1/M), apart from logarithmic factors, where M is the feature count. The results cover both the kernel function and its associated integral operator. The stronger rate means the approximation error decreases faster as more features are used within the analyzed class.

The paper also studies kernel ridge regression, proving that fewer features can suffice to preserve the same convergence rate of excess risk. Empirical results support better performance, and the approach is described as straightforward to implement. Together, these findings connect an improvement in kernel approximation to a potential reduction in the representation needed for a downstream learning task.
icml-2024-quasi-monte-carlo-features-for.tldr: For a kernel class including Gaussian kernels, quasi-Monte Carlo features improve approximation rates and can reduce feature requirements in kernel ridge regression.

paragraphs: Federated learning can be disrupted by malicious clients that upload deliberately harmful updates. Existing robust aggregation approaches can depend on similar client-data distributions or related proxy datasets. Self-Driven Entropy Aggregation, or SDEA, addresses aggregation with heterogeneous client data using a random public dataset.

The method starts from the observation that benign clients typically make sharper, more confident predictions than malicious clients on that public data. It learns aggregation weights by minimizing the global model’s prediction entropy for individual examples. However, honest clients also differ in confidence because their local training distributions differ. Favoring only the sharpest predictions can therefore overemphasize a small subset of honest clients.

SDEA counterbalances that tendency by maximizing prediction entropy across a batch, encouraging diverse overall predictions. It also uses clustering to distribute honest-client weights equally across differing tendencies. Empirical results support the resulting defense in heterogeneous federated learning. The key idea is that confidence can help identify useful contributions, but it needs a diversity mechanism to avoid confusing legitimate client differences with poor contributions.
icml-2024-self-driven-entropy-aggregatio.tldr: SDEA balances prediction confidence and diversity on public data to aggregate heterogeneous federated updates while resisting malicious clients.

paragraphs: Online change detection aims to identify changes in a data stream promptly, with applications such as smart-grid security and network intrusion detection. Many existing approaches assume system parameters are known precisely. The paper challenges that premise because parameter estimates can be inaccurate and systems can change after those estimates are obtained.

Triadic-OCD is proposed as a framework combining certifiable robustness, provable optimality, and guaranteed convergence. Its algorithm can run in a fully asynchronous distributed manner, reducing the need to collect data at one server. Asynchronous operation could also reduce the effects of slow participants that delay progress in synchronous algorithms.

The authors analyze non-asymptotic convergence and derive the iteration complexity needed to reach an epsilon-optimal point, meaning a solution within a specified tolerance of optimality. Experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution brings together uncertainty-aware change detection and distributed computation, with theory addressing finite-iteration progress rather than only eventual convergence. Its asynchronous design provides an additional route for handling practical differences in participants’ processing speeds.
icml-2024-triadic-ocd-asynchronous-onlin.tldr: Triadic-OCD combines robust online change detection with asynchronous distributed execution and theoretical optimality and convergence guarantees.
